hints: Focus on why solid AgBr needs to be washed off the film, and what kind of product would wash away easily in water.
Check the oxidation number of silver and bromine on both sides, in AgBr and in Br- and [Ag(S2O3)2]3-.
Notice how thiosulfate ends up bonded to silver in a charged complex ion, think about what that does to solubility.
walkthrough:
**See the practical problem**

Think like a photographer. Unreacted AgBr is an insoluble solid stuck on the film. To remove it, you must turn it into something water soluble that can be washed away.

Starting material:
$$\text{AgBr(s) insoluble}$$

**Test for redox by checking oxidation numbers**

A good chemist always checks if oxidation or reduction happened. In AgBr, Ag is +1 and Br is -1.

In products, in $\text{Br}^-$ Br is still -1, and in $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$ Ag is still +1. Nothing is oxidised or reduced.
$$\text{Ag(+I) } \rightarrow \text{ Ag(+I)}, \quad \text{Br(-I) } \rightarrow \text{ Br(-I)}$$

**Recognise complex formation**

Since there is no redox, the thiosulfate ion $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ must be acting as a ligand. It bonds to $\text{Ag}^+$ to form the soluble complex ion $[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$.

$$\text{Ag}^+ + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]^{3-}$$
This soluble complex washes off the film, so the function is to make the silver ions soluble.

options.A: Correct. AgBr is insoluble. Thiosulfate acts as a ligand to form the soluble complex [Ag(S2O3)2]3-, which dissolves in water and can be washed off the film. No change in oxidation number occurs.
options.B: Incorrect. Oxidation would mean an increase in oxidation number. Silver stays as +1 in both AgBr and in the complex [Ag(S2O3)2]3-, so no oxidation takes place. This traps students who assume any reaction with an ion must be redox.
options.C: Incorrect. Bromine is -1 in AgBr and -1 in Br-, so its oxidation number does not change. It is simply released as bromide ion when the lattice breaks up, not reduced.
options.D: Incorrect. Reduction would mean a decrease in oxidation number, for example Ag+ to Ag metal. Here silver remains +1 throughout, so no reduction occurs. This is a complex formation (ligand exchange) reaction, not redox.
